r.t: Vowels in unstressed words (e.g. סע = עס, מע, זשע) are never long, and usually reduced to /ə/.

Length distinction for [e, u, i] is neutralized before [ng, nk], though the precise realization seems to differ by variety and the linguist describing it. In the database, they are consistently marked as short for convenience.

This guide does NOT cover אַ vs ײַ (i.e. short vs. long [a]), as this is immediately apparent graphically. It also does not cover the more limited CY phenomenon of אַ representing /aː/ in certain words borrowed from German, e.g. פּלאַן.

A number of words have been imported from modern German that have long /oː/ in German. Their nativization into Yiddish varies by subdialect and the individual word, and can range from simply short /ɔ/ to long /oː/ or even long /uː/. These are marked in the database in the “Notes” column. Examples include מיליאָן, (דער) טאָן, מאָדע.
In CY, long [o] has three different realizations:
Diphthongized /uːə/ when preceding [d, t, n, l, r] in a closed syllable, e.g. ר
/buːərt/, מאָל /muːəl/. The “offglide schwa” can also be heard in long [i] preceding [r]. However, this schwa is not found in all CY, it is notably absent in HHY.
/ before labials and velars, e.g. זקן, געגראָבן, בחור, שלאָפֿן (regionally, שטראָפֿן is an exception, with /uː/).
Words of newer vintage with [u] are often pronounced as /u/, and not as /ɪ/ or /i/: שטורעם (/shturəm/), גרופּע (/grupə/),  פּובליקום (/publɪkum/). These words are marked as such in the database.
Long [e] does not appear before [kh]. Additionally, some parts of SEY have no length distinction in the sequence [er]: װער (CY /veɪ̯ər/, SEY /vɛɪ̯r/ or /vɛr/).
Examples of vowel lowering before [r, kh]: קורץ (CY /kɔrts/, SEY /kɛrts/), קירצער (/kɛrtsər/), פּוך (CY /pɔkh/, SEY /pɛkh/), ליכט (/lɛkht/).
Vowel lowering has gone further in some parts of CY, where /ɛr/ — whether from underlying יר or ער — is pronounced /ar/ (same for /ɛkh/), e.g.
.  The database contains some 40 examples; see items marked “
Lowering does not apply to words of newer vintage, e.g. װיכטיק /vikhtɪk/ or /vɪkhtɪk/, שטורעם /shturem/.

rules.c: See "key verbs and "key patterns".
The vowel does not carry (primary or secondary) word stress.  See also section on pronouns, which often have different pronunciations based on stress.
The sequence transcribed [oye], [oyi], or [oi] where the first part of the diphthong is represented by a komets, not by a vov or khoylem.
The transcribed vowel is either word-final or followed by another vowel.
The vowel is immediately followed by א, ה, ע. (The ה may be non-silent in the transcription.)

The vowel in the transcription is either followed by 1 consonant word-finally, or by 2 consonants word-medially, where the second consonant can be <י> or even silent <ע, א, ה> — but not syllabic <נ> or <ל>.
The vowel is transcribed as [e].
The vowel is transcribed as [o] (excluding [oy]).
The vowel is followed by <ב, כּ, פּ, תּ>.
The vowel is followed by <בֿ, כ, פֿ, ת>.
The vowel is followed by ר or ח (plus another vowel).
The vowel is followed by a consonant that is written in Masoretic Hebrew with a dagesh. Common patterns include CiCuC

The word is a noun (plural, feminine, possessive, etc.) or adjective derived from a base noun, where the base is consonant-final but in the derivation that consonant is followed by a vowel. (May or may not be accompanied by a shift in syllable stress.) Does not include diminutives.
All other derivations, including diminutives, other derived nouns (plural, feminine, possessive), prefixed forms, adjectives, verbs, etc.
After applying all the above rules, assume the vowel in the remaining words is long.

If you revert the word to its bare root (after removing affixes and undoing plurals, diminutives, conjugations, etc.), the stressed vowel either remains the same, or is related via a stem change of [e] < [o, a] or [i] < [u].
rules.d: Same length as in base form. [a] is considered short.

rules.b: From now on, apply all rules to the root.

rules.c: The word is of Slavic origin, which may feature telltale signs such as: ending in unstressed <ע>; suffixes <יק> or <עק>; consonants like <זש> and <טש>; palatalized consonants; and unusual consonant combinations. (This rule is only marked in the database when not covered by any of the subsequent rules.)
Borrowings from English. In HHY, English "u"/"oo" is often represented by <א> or <אָ>, competing with the older/mainstream standard of using <ו> on the basis of NEY pronunciation.
Any vowel followed by another vowel or root boundary.
The vowel <ע> or <אָ>, followed by <ס> or <כ>.
The sequence <אָר> followed by dental consonant <ד, ט, נ, ל>, vowel, or root boundary.
Any other vowel, i.e. <ו, י, ע>, followed by <ר> and a root boundary.
The sequence <ער> followed by a dental consonant <ד, ט, נ, ל> or a vowel.
Any other sequence of a vowel followed by <ר> and a consonant.
Any vowel followed by three consonants, or by two consonants and a root boundary — provided the second consonant is not syllabic, i.e. <ל> or <נ>.
A vowel followed by <מ, נ, ל> and another consonant. The second consonant may be syllabic.
A vowel followed by 1-2 consonants and a <י>. These words are often Slavic.
A vowel plus one of the following: <פּ, פֿ, ק, צ, טש, ש, דזש, זש>.
The vowel <י> or <ו>, followed by <מ>.
The vowel sequence <עב> or <יד>
The vowel <ע> or <אָ>, plus one of the following: <ג, ד, װ, ז>. Applies only to words from the Germanic component.
